representation.name: representation
representation.definition: A learned numerical description used by a later computation.
representation.explanation: A representation turns an input into features or coordinates that make some relationships easier to use. Its value depends on the downstream question. A code that reconstructs every nuisance detail may be poor for classification, while a contrastive code may discard information needed for reconstruction. Dimension alone does not establish usefulness. Evaluate a representation with a declared task, such as reconstruction error, paired retrieval, a frozen linear probe, or transfer to held-out labels.

autoencoder.name: autoencoder
autoencoder.definition: An encoder-decoder model trained to reconstruct a target derived from its input.
autoencoder.explanation: The encoder maps input features to a code and the decoder maps that code back to the target space. In clean reconstruction, the input values also supply the reconstruction targets; a denoising autoencoder instead receives corrupted features with clean targets. This chapter's loss is coordinate MSE, averaged over rows times coordinates. A constrained code can capture recurring structure, but an unconstrained model can learn a near-identity mapping. Reconstruction success therefore measures reconstruction, not universal representation quality.

bottleneck.name: bottleneck
bottleneck.explanation: A bottleneck has fewer coordinates, lower capacity, or another constraint that prevents an encoder from copying its input trivially. In this chapter, four input values become two tanh coordinates before decoding. The restriction encourages compression but does not identify a unique coordinate system: several rotations or sign changes can reconstruct equally well. A bottleneck that is too narrow loses relevant information, while one that is too wide may simply memorize small training data.

contrastive-learning.name: contrastive learning
contrastive-learning.definition: Representation learning that rewards matching views relative to nonmatching examples.
contrastive-learning.explanation: Contrastive training starts with positive pairs, such as two transformations of the same item, and negatives drawn from other items. An encoder produces vectors whose similarities become logits. The objective raises the positive logit relative to the alternatives. The learned invariances come from how views are constructed, so bad augmentations teach the wrong equivalence. Negative selection, batch composition, temperature, and evaluation protocol materially affect the result.

infonce.name: InfoNCE
infonce.definition: A softmax contrastive loss that identifies a positive candidate among negatives.
infonce.explanation: For one anchor, divide similarities by a positive temperature and treat them as logits. The loss is log-sum-exp over every candidate logit minus the positive logit. Subtracting the maximum before exponentiation makes the calculation stable; clamping probabilities changes the objective. This chapter averages over anchors without another candidate-count division, and its gradient uses the same denominator while accumulating both branches of the shared encoder. Six in-batch candidates teach the mechanism but do not reproduce large-batch studies.
